zh_summary: (Reposted by @robin_j_brooks) @ManuelSamuel：海灣原油流量已恢復至戰前91%，但成品油出口仍低於50%（IEA）；運費達每桶34美元，荷姆茲戰爭風險溢價高企，市場分割纔是更大問題。
text:
The Gulf Oil Paradox: Restoring Crude Is Not Restoring Fuel

@robin_j_brooks is right to highlight the IRGC's impact on freight, but the bigger story is market fragmentation. Gulf crude flows have recovered to 91% of pre-war levels; refined-product exports remain below 50% (IEA). Freight has hit $34/bbl and Hormuz war-risk premiums 6–9% of hull value. Oil can flow while diesel stays scarce and expensive. The risk premium is not just military: it's embedded in damaged refineries, thin inventories and a global tanker shortage.

name: jeroen blokland
zh_summary: @jsblokland：投資幾乎都圍繞名義回報，但經歷史上最嚴重的債券熊市之一後，要回溯30年才找到債券累計實際回報為正的時期。
text:
It is rather remarkable that nearly everything in investing revolves around nominal returns.

Institutional investors determine their strategic asset allocation largely on the basis of nominal data.

Following one of the worst bond bear markets on record, you now have to go back 30 years to find a positive cumulative real return on bonds.

Many investors simply do not realize that three decades of real returns from bond investing have effectively been wiped out.

That does not mean bonds cannot perform well from here, especially now that real yields have turned positive again.

But if you were to use real returns in a standard mean-variance optimization model, as most institutional investors do, there is virtually no chance that bonds would receive an allocation anywhere near 40% in the strategic asset mix.

In fact, bonds receive no allocation at all once you expand the investment universe beyond different types of stocks and bonds.

And the outlook for bonds, something that is almost never incorporated into traditional mean-variance optimization models, becomes significantly less attractive when you factor in the prospect of higher inflation.
